entity.name: Marie Curie
entity.description: The first woman to win a Nobel Prize and the only person to win Nobels in two different sciences (Physics 1903, Chemistry 1911). Discovered radium in a leaking shed. Her notebooks are still too radioactive to handle without protection.

story.name: Marie Curie
story.description: Studies at a clandestine university in occupied Warsaw, nearly starves in a Paris garret, discovers two elements, drives X-ray trucks to the front in WWI, and dies from the radiation that made her famous.

moments.name: Maria Sklodowska Is Born in Russian-Occupied Warsaw
moments.subtitle: The fifth child of teachers in a Poland that does not officially exist on any map
moments.description: On November 7, 1867, Maria Salomea Sklodowska was born in Warsaw, then part of the Russian Empire's Congress Poland. Her parents were both teachers who had lost their family fortunes through patriotic involvement in Polish uprisings. Her father Wladyslaw taught mathematics and physics; her mother Bronislawa ran a prestigious boarding school. After Russian authorities banned laboratory instruction in Polish schools, Maria's father brought equipment home and taught his children himself. Maria's mother died of tuberculosis when Maria was 10, and her oldest sister Zofia died of typhus. These losses turned her away from Catholicism and toward science.

moments.name: Marie Sklodowska Arrives in Paris to Study Physics at the Sorbonne
moments.subtitle: Denied university education in Poland for being a woman, she crosses Europe to learn
moments.description: In late 1891, 24-year-old Maria Sklodowska left Poland for Paris, following her elder sister Bronislawa. She enrolled at the University of Paris (the Sorbonne) to study physics, chemistry, and mathematics. Sklodowska rented a garret in the Latin Quarter and lived in extreme poverty, sometimes forgetting to eat because she was so absorbed in study. She kept warm by wearing every piece of clothing she owned. In 1893, she earned a degree in physics, and in 1894 a degree in mathematics. That same year she met Pierre Curie, the physicist who would become her husband and research partner. Poland had denied her a university place; France gave her two Nobel Prizes.
moments.address: University of Paris, Latin Quarter, Paris

moments.name: Marie Curie Drives Mobile X-Ray Units to World War I Battlefields
moments.subtitle: A Nobel laureate loads radiology equipment into trucks and heads for the trenches
moments.description: During World War I, beginning in 1914, Marie Curie developed mobile radiography units -- nicknamed 'petites Curies' -- to provide X-ray services to field hospitals near the front lines. Curie learned to drive, studied anatomy, and trained other women as X-ray operators. She equipped approximately 20 vehicles with X-ray equipment and established 200 fixed radiological units. The technology allowed surgeons to locate bullets and shrapnel in wounded soldiers, saving countless lives. Curie also trained her teenage daughter Irene to operate the equipment at the front. The radiation exposure from this wartime work likely contributed to the aplastic anemia that eventually killed her.

moments.name: Marie Curie Founds the Radium Institute in Paris
moments.subtitle: A research center built for one scientist becomes a factory for Nobel Prize winners
moments.description: In 1920, Marie Curie founded the Radium Institute (Institut du Radium, now Institut Curie) in Paris, dedicated to research in physics, chemistry, and medical applications of radioactivity. The institute was built on Rue Pierre et Marie Curie, named after the couple. Under Curie's direction, the institute conducted the world's first studies on treating tumors with radioactive isotopes. The institute became one of the most important research centers in the world, producing four Nobel Prize winners. Curie directed the institute until her death in 1934. It remains a major medical research center today, at the forefront of cancer treatment.
moments.address: Rue Pierre et Marie Curie, Paris, France

moments.name: Marie Curie Dies from the Radiation That Made Her Famous
moments.subtitle: Her own discovery killed her, and her notebooks remain radioactive a century later
moments.description: On July 4, 1934, Marie Curie died at the Sancellemoz sanatorium in Passy, Haute-Savoie, France, at age 66. The cause was aplastic anemia, almost certainly caused by years of exposure to radiation during her research and her World War I radiological work. Curie had carried test tubes of radioactive isotopes in her pockets and stored them in her desk drawer. In 1995, she became the first woman interred on her own merits in the Paris Pantheon. Her personal papers from the 1890s, including cookbooks, are still so contaminated with radium-226 that they must be kept in lead-lined boxes and require protective clothing to handle.
